transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, occupational health sent me, really. They’re saying I’m not eating enough. I mean, I don’t think it’s as dramatic as they make it sound, but most days I’ll just have black coffee, maybe a plain yogurt, and then at night a few bites of chicken or something.

It’s just… a full meal feels like I’m letting my standards slip. I know that probably sounds odd. In my line of work you learn discipline matters—though honestly, half the guys at the station live on takeout and complain about being tired all day—but for me, eating more than that feels like losing control. So that’s why I’m here, I guess.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'letting my standards slip' and 'losing control' when it comes to eating more?

I mean… it’s not just the food, exactly. It’s what it says about me afterward. If I eat a full meal, then I’ll catch myself checking in the mirror, especially my stomach and my waist, and I can’t really see what other people say they see. They’ll say I look fine, or lean, or whatever, but I just see where it looks soft.

And then the whole day gets judged by that, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud. Like, I can handle a chaotic call or paperwork stacked to the ceiling, but if I look in the mirror and don’t look… tight enough, disciplined enough, then I feel like I’ve failed somehow. Like I don’t respect myself. My wife used to say I was harder on myself than anyone on the force ever was, and maybe that’s true, but it’s hard to switch off.
After eating, do you ever make yourself exercise more than you planned, make yourself vomit, or do anything else to try to 'undo' the food you ate?

I don’t know… I mean, “undo” sounds like a strong word. I don’t really think of it that way.

Sometimes after eating I get restless, but then again I’ve always been someone who needs to move around. Sitting still after dinner feels strange to me—my dad was like that too, always fixing something in the garage after meals, couldn’t just watch television like a normal person. So I don’t know if that counts as exercise or just… habit.

As for the other thing, making myself sick, I don’t—no, I don’t think so. I’ve never really been that kind of person. I’m more the type to just keep things tight in the first place, if that makes sense.
Can you tell me if you ever feel you need to work off what you eat, or if you exercise more than most people would consider normal to manage your weight or shape?

I’m not sure I’d call it “work off,” exactly. I mean, I do like being active, but I don’t know what most people would consider normal anymore. In the job, you’re always moving, or you used to be—I’m behind a desk more now than I’d like, which is its own kind of frustration.

I suppose if I’ve eaten more than I meant to, I don’t feel great just sitting there. I’ll get up, do something around the house, take care of things that need doing. But then my neighbor, he’s retired fire service, he walks miles every day and nobody says that’s odd, they say he’s keeping himself in shape. So I don’t really know where the line is.

I guess I don’t think of it as managing weight or shape so much as not letting myself get sloppy. But… I don’t know. Maybe that’s splitting hairs.
Do your concerns about your weight or body shape interfere with your daily life, such as affecting your work, relationships, or other important areas of functioning?

Yeah… I suppose it does, more than I’d like to admit.

Work-wise, occupational health has been holding up my clearance for field-related duties, and that’s… not nothing. In my line of work, once people start wondering if you’re fit to be out there, it changes how they look at you. I can tell the team is second-guessing me a bit, even if they don’t say it outright. You get used to reading people, you know—body language, little pauses, who gets asked to do what. After enough years, you notice.

And socially, I’ve pretty much stopped meeting people for meals. I’ll say I’m busy, or I already ate, or suggest coffee instead. It’s easier than sitting there with people watching what I order, making comments, trying to push food on me. My old shift used to do these breakfasts after nights, and that was sort of sacred, really—half the job happened in those booths—but now I just avoid it. So yes, I guess it has gotten in the way.

When you look at yourself in the mirror and notice areas that seem 'soft,' is this something you feel is a realistic reflection of your actual body, or do you think you're seeing yourself differently than others might?

I mean… I know people keep saying I’m seeing it wrong, but when I look, it feels pretty real to me.

It’s usually my stomach, my waist. That’s where my eyes go first. I can be getting dressed for the day, just trying to put on a shirt, and if it looks… soft, or not tight enough, then that sets the tone for everything. It’s stupid, because I’ve stood in front of mirrors in locker rooms for years, uniforms, body armor, all that—everyone joking about getting older, bad backs, who’s gone up a belt notch. Normal stuff.

But for me it doesn’t feel normal. I don’t really see what everyone else says they see. I see that part, and then somehow that becomes the whole picture. If I don’t look lean enough, I feel like I’ve failed before the day’s even started. Like I can’t really respect myself properly.

When you look at yourself and feel like you appear 'soft' or not lean enough, even when others tell you you're fine, do you believe that your view of your body is accurate, or do you think you might be misjudging your actual appearance?

I’d like to say I might be misjudging it, because that’s the sensible answer, isn’t it? That’s what everyone seems to be waiting for me to say.

But when I’m actually standing there, looking in the mirror, it doesn’t feel like a mistake. My eyes go straight to my stomach, my waist, and if that looks soft to me, then… that’s all I can see. It’s like the rest of me doesn’t count.

I know other people say I look fine, but I don’t really see what they’re talking about. I judge the whole thing by whether I look lean enough, and if I don’t, it affects how I feel about myself for the day. Like I can’t quite respect myself properly.
Would you say that your view of your body—especially your stomach and waist—is something that you base a lot of your overall self-worth on?

Yeah… I think that’s fair to say. More than I’d like, honestly.

It’s not like I wake up and make some formal decision—“right, today my worth depends on my waist,” you know—but that is sort of what happens. I look in the mirror, and my eyes go straight there. Stomach, waist. If it looks soft to me, then the whole day feels… off. Like I’m already losing before I’ve even left the house.

And I know people say they don’t see what I see. I’ve heard that enough times. But when I’m looking at myself, I don’t see what they’re talking about. I just see whether I look lean enough, and if I don’t, it’s hard to feel like I can respect myself properly.

It sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud. I’ve dealt with plenty of real things in my job, things that actually matter, and yet I can stand there getting hung up on a bit of softness around my middle like it’s some kind of character flaw. But yes… I suppose I do base too much of how I feel about myself on that.

Would you say that your concern about your stomach and waist is mainly about controlling your weight and shape, or is it more about a specific dissatisfaction with how that part of your body looks, even if others don’t seem to notice anything wrong?

I think it’s both, maybe… but mostly it comes down to how that part looks to me. My stomach, my waist — that’s where I get stuck.

I can tell myself it’s about being disciplined or staying in shape, and, you know, in my job you get used to checking things — your uniform, your belt, whether everything sits right. Even after years, you notice if something feels off. But this isn’t really the same as making sure your shirt’s tucked in properly. I’ll look in the mirror and I don’t see what everyone else says they see.

My eyes just go straight there, and if I think I look soft or not lean enough, then it sort of ruins the whole picture. Doesn’t matter if someone else says I look fine. I judge the day by it, almost. If my waist looks wrong to me, I feel like I can’t respect myself the same way.
Even though others say you look fine or lean, do you see yourself as underweight, or do you feel that you still need to lose more weight to look the way you want?

I don’t really see myself the way other people describe me, no. If someone says I look fine or lean, I can hear the words, but when I’m in front of the mirror it’s like they don’t apply.

I don’t stand there thinking, “I’m underweight,” if that’s what you mean. My eyes just go straight to my stomach and waist, and if that area looks soft to me, then the rest of it doesn’t matter. It’s funny, well—not funny—but in the force you get used to noticing tiny things out of place, a crease, a belt sitting wrong, boots not polished properly. And I think I’ve taken that sort of inspection and turned it on myself.

So… yes, I suppose I feel like I still need to be leaner to look right. Or at least to feel right. If I don’t look lean enough there, I end up judging the whole day by it, like I can’t quite respect myself.

inference_history.note: The patient presents with restricted eating and a sense of losing control related to food intake, which raises suspicion for an eating disorder. Specific focus on discipline and appearance of symptoms in the context of occupational factors opens consideration for Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00), Binge Eating Disorder (F50.81), or Other Specified Eating or Eating Disorders (F50.89). No further information is available to narrow the differential at this point.

This turn ruled out F50.89 as the patient denies making themselves vomit or engaging in compensatory behaviors such as excessive exercise specifically to undo food intake. The focus remains on restrictive eating and body image concerns, supporting the continuation of F50.00 (Anorexia nervosa) and F50.81 (Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder) as candidates.
